headline: AMD MI355X crushes NVIDIA B300 on Kimi K3 performance per dollar, running at 952 tok/s/node
summary: AMD's MI355X GPUs deliver superior performance per dollar for the massive 2.8T parameter Kimi K3 model, outperforming NVIDIA's B300 despite software challenges.
details: The open-source Kimi K3 model, with 2.8 trillion parameters, requires over 1.5TB of VRAM, making it too large for a single NVIDIA B200 node. This necessitates high-capacity GPUs like NVIDIA's B300 or multiple B200 nodes.
AMD's MI355X GPUs offer 288GB of VRAM, comparable to the B300, but are approximately 2.4 times cheaper per GPU. This positions them as a cost-efficient alternative to NVIDIA's Blackwell series.

Benchmarking Kimi K3 on MI355X yields 952 tokens/second/node, with 118 tokens/second single stream. This is significantly higher than a two-node B200 deployment, which achieved 249 tokens/second/node.

While B300 nodes still achieve higher aggregate throughput (1.65x), their 2.4x higher price means the MI355X offers a much better performance-per-dollar ratio. The MI355X costs $2.50/GPU-hr compared to $6.00 for the B300.
Historically, AMD has faced software support challenges for frontier models. However, with day-0 support for Kimi K3, much of the initial engineering effort for deployment was mitigated.

Further optimization involved fixing speculative decode issues on ROCm, which required a PyTorch function correction. This simple fix, addressing a missing definition rather than a missing kernel, significantly boosted performance.

The speculative decode fix resulted in a 2.2x gain in single-stream performance and an 18% increase in peak aggregate throughput. This also allowed for much higher concurrency, demonstrating the MI355X's practical edge in HBM capacity for large models.

headline_marked: [[125M model beats 14B LLM]] at medical text de-identification, 40x faster on CPU
headline: 125M model beats 14B LLM at medical text de-identification, 40x faster on CPU
summary: A new local-first tool, localscrub, uses a compact 125-million-parameter model to de-identify medical text 40 times faster than a 14-billion-parameter LLM, all on a consumer CPU.
details: A new open-source project, localscrub, introduces a local-first PHI (Protected Health Information) de-identification cascade. Its 125-million-parameter model achieved 40 times faster performance than a 14-billion-parameter LLM in de-identifying medical text, all while running on a consumer laptop's CPU.

Current methods force a trade-off: cloud APIs are accurate but send sensitive data off-premises, while local rule-based tools keep data home but often miss context-dependent PHI. localscrub aims to solve this by performing all processing on local hardware, ensuring data privacy.

The tool employs a two-stage cascade: a fast rules-and-NER pass handles well-formatted identifiers, and a local LLM (Qwen3:14b via Ollama) processes the ambiguous remainder. Crucially, no network egress is involved, keeping all sensitive data within the user's trust boundary.

To ensure robust benchmarking without using real PHI, localscrub generates synthetic clinical notes with fabricated identifiers. This deterministic approach allows the test set to be a function rather than a static file, enabling verifiable accuracy claims.

A unique `--diversify` feature allows a local LLM to paraphrase connective prose around masked identifiers, preventing template memorization by the detector. This validation loop ensures the LLM doesn't invent PHI or corrupt the ground truth, maintaining test set integrity.

The `localscrub eval` harness reports three distinct metrics per entity type, with Redaction Recall serving as the critical safety metric. This detailed reporting helped identify issues like partial redactions, which are still considered data leaks, ensuring comprehensive protection.
